items.title: From archive to resource: bringing legacy data back to life at scale with large language models
items.abstract: Pharmaceutical companies maintain vast archives of legacy preclinical study reports that contain study-context details, such as fasting, anesthesia, and laboratory instrumentation, that are rarely captured in structured data formats, yet they can correlate with clinical pathology parameters values and limit the reuse of historical data. This work demonstrates practical, scalable solutions to recover such descriptors from heterogeneous report texts using large language model (LLM)-based extraction pipelines developed independently by two industry teams. The pipelines identify and normalize metadata fields and return verbatim evidence with page and section reference, hasting human verification and iterative refinement. Evaluation of over 400 documents against expert-curated reference values showed high agreement across a broad set of metadata fields. Performance was strongest for consistently reported items and lower for descriptors subject to linguistic or report structure variability. Extraction time has shrunk from 25 minutes in the manual benchmark to 1.6 minutes. As a concrete biological demonstration, we show that fasting status extracted from report text was associated with species- and analyte-specific shifts in clinical chemistry parameters, illustrating how recovered metadata can improve selection of historical controls. Key strengths of the approach are scalability, traceability, and the ability to recover information missing from current industry standards. Main limitations are dependence on source-report quality and initial expert effort to define and refine schemas. These results establish how LLMs can convert heterogeneous, unstructured legacy reports into evidence-grounded, reusable and structured metadata, leading to better experimental comparability, and thus enabling reliable data pooling or informed virtual control selection.

items.title: From Atoms to Reactors: A Critical Review of a Decade of Machine Learning in Heterogeneous Catalysis (2017–2026)
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This critical review traces the evolution of machine learning (ML) across the full value chain of heterogeneous catalysis over 2017–2026, from catalyst discovery to reactor and process design, and across the principal reaction families (CO 2 reduction, water splitting, nitrogen chemistry, zeolite‐catalyzed transformations). Each stage is evaluated against four criteria — data foundation, method maturity, experimental validation and deployment readiness — through a structured capability scorecard. Digitalization has advanced from the top of the length scale downward: prediction of adsorption energies and atomistic potential‐energy surfaces is now mature, with errors of tens of meV relative to the reference DFT calculations and accelerations of three orders of magnitude over DFT, yet experimentally validated catalyst improvements remain rare. The most significant advance is the closed‐loop autonomous laboratory coupling Bayesian optimization, automated synthesis and high‐throughput testing. Large language models have begun to add a reasoning and orchestration layer, while kinetics, reactor and process design remain the least digitalized stages. We argue that the field's next decade of impact will be decided not by more accurate atomic‐scale prediction but by carrying ML into experimental validation and the reactor‐and‐process scale, where catalysis is hardest to industrialize and where data‐driven methods are weakest.

items.title: From Automation to Augmentation: Artificial Intelligence, Competence Evolution, and Career Sustainability in the Accounting Profession
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the content of accounting work, but the career consequences of that change remain less clear in emerging economies. Using field responses from 600 accounting and finance professionals in Nigeria, Ghana, and Kenya (200 per country), this paper examines whether intensive AI use is associated with professional role transformation, whether role transformation is associated with competence evolution, and whether those evolving competencies are linked to career sustainability. Learning and organizational support is considered both as a contextual resource and as a potential moderator. The analysis uses multi-item composite measures, HC3-robust path regressions, 5,000-resample bootstrapping, effect-size estimates, 10-fold cross-validation, and exploratory country comparisons. AI adoption was positively associated with role transformation (β = .491, p < .001). AI adoption (β = .286, p < .001) and role transformation (β = .462, p < .001) jointly explained 42.6% of the variance in competence evolution, while competence evolution was positively associated with career sustainability (β = .414, p < .001). The direct role-transformation effect on career sustainability was negligible (β = .013, p = .764), whereas the indirect effect through competence evolution was significant (β = .192, 95% bootstrap CI [.146, .242]). The serial pathway from AI adoption through role transformation and competence evolution to career sustainability was also significant (β = .094, 95% CI [.069, .123]). Learning and organizational support had a positive main effect but did not moderate the competence-sustainability relationship. The results suggest that the long-term value of AI-related role change depends less on the fact that work changes than on whether professionals acquire the digital, analytical, advisory, and ethical capabilities needed to succeed in the redesigned role. Keywords: artificial intelligence; accounting profession; role transformation; competence evolution; career sustainability; emerging economies; Africa; human capital.

items.title: From awareness to trust: a social work perspective on occupational accident rights, employee voice, and safety performance
items.abstract: This study examines the associations among occupational health and safety awareness, OHS performance, employee voice, and organizational trust from a social work perspective. Although previous studies have examined occupational health and safety, employee voice, and organizational trust separately, limited attention has been paid to how these variables operate together within a rights-based and empowerment-oriented social work framework. Data collected from 400 factory employees were analyzed using correlation analysis, multiple regression analysis, and PROCESS Model 6. The findings showed that greater awareness was significantly associated with organizational trust through both direct and indirect pathways. OHS performance and employee voice were significant mediators, and the sequential indirect effect through OHS performance and employee voice was statistically significant. Rather than introducing previously unexamined associations, the study integrates established workplace variables within a sequential model and interprets their combined relevance for rights-based education, employee participation, and workplace social work practice.

items.title: From Data to Decision-Making: A Review of Large Language Model Applications Across the Full Lifecycle of Geothermal Resource Development
items.abstract: Geothermal resource development involves heterogeneous geological and engineering records, uncertain reservoir parameters, and decisions constrained by physical processes and safety requirements. This narrative and critical review examines how large language models (LLMs), including retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted systems, could support knowledge-intensive tasks throughout geothermal exploration, development, and operation. It distinguishes direct geothermal evidence from empirical evaluations in adjacent fields and from conceptual proposals; results from petroleum engineering, mineral exploration, and broader energy systems are not treated as proof of geothermal performance. Peer-reviewed studies demonstrate useful capabilities in technical document extraction, domain question answering, knowledge-graph reasoning, and interactions with scientific software, but direct geothermal engineering validation remains limited. For reservoir inversion, drilling-risk warning, and design optimization, quantitative assessment must rely on measured data and validated physical or numerical models, with LLMs acting as auditable interfaces and information-integration tools. The review proposes a task-specific benchmark framework and examines cross-domain transfer, multimodal alignment, knowledge-graph and retrieval collaboration, uncertainty quantification, and LLM–physical-model coupling. These frameworks are literature-informed proposals rather than implemented geothermal systems. Key priorities include independent geothermal test sets, expert-annotated reference answers, calibrated uncertainty, physics-based verification, and transparent reporting of model failure. The resulting synthesis identifies credible current applications and the evidence requirements for reliable future deployment.

items.title: From Instrument to Economic Actor: Generative and Agentic AI as a New Logic of Business Model Innovation
items.abstract: (1) Background: Generative and, increasingly, agentic artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping how firms create, deliver, and capture value. Yet business model innovation (BMI) research often assumes that humans retain design authority while digital technologies support analysis or execute predefined decisions. This assumption becomes contestable when AI systems can generate value-bearing artifacts, participate in organizational decision-making, and undertake goal-directed action within delegated boundaries. (2) Approach: Integrating business-model and activity-system research, dynamic capabilities, socio-technical and human–AI decision-making perspectives, and research on generative and agentic AI, this concept paper develops a framework that distinguishes three logics of AI-enabled BMI: a supporting logic (AI as instrument), a generative logic (AI as co-creator), and an agentic logic (AI as delegated economic actor). The framework distinguishes business-model operation from business-model innovation and identifies delegated reconfiguration authority as a key condition under which agentic action can constitute BMI. (3) Contribution: The paper advances six propositions explaining how AI redistributes ideation, decision, execution, and reconfiguration rights; how machine agency may compress the interval between business-model reconfigurations; how value-capture mechanisms may change; and why complementary capabilities, governance, and legitimacy remain decisive. (4) Conclusions: The paper offers a focused research agenda centered on agency allocation and decision rights, the temporal dynamics and measurement of BMI, and value capture and governance in agent-mediated business models. It thereby provides a more precise theoretical basis for distinguishing autonomous operation within a business model from autonomous or semi-autonomous reconfiguration of the business model itself.

items.title: From Natural Equality to Constitutional Legitimacy: Locke’s Political Anthropology and Algorithmic Governance
items.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence into governance challenges the conditions under which political authority can be considered legitimate. Algorithmic systems increasingly mediate decisions that shape citizens’ lives, yet their operations frequently bypass human judgment and obscure the justificatory basis of political authority. This article reinterprets John Locke’s political philosophy as a normative framework for assessing algorithmic authority. By reconstructing Locke’s account of reason, equality, consent, and fiduciary trust, it brings his political anthropology into dialogue with contemporary debates on algorithmic accountability and digital constitutionalism. The article argues that AI governance does not merely raise technical or regulatory problems; it threatens the conditions under which citizens can understand, evaluate, and contest the exercise of power. Because many AI systems operate through models that neither officials nor citizens can meaningfully interpret, they generate forms of automated prerogative that weaken the fiduciary relationship between governors and governed. Against this danger, the article advances a Lockean criterion for computational governance: algorithmic authority can be considered legitimate only insofar as it preserves intelligibility, fiduciary accountability, and contestability. Legitimacy cannot be restored through technical adjustment alone; it requires institutional conditions under which power remains publicly intelligible, politically answerable, and open to challenge by those subject to it.

items.title: From Noisy Retrieval to Decision Evidence: Silver Evidence Demonstrations for In-Context Learning
items.abstract: RAG and retrieval-augmented few-shot ICL can struggle when decision-relevant evidence is buried in long, noisy context. Retrieved passages and demonstrations may contain redundant or distracting information. Although expert-labeled development examples may identify the text supporting each decision, these annotations are typically used only as answer-side rationales rather than as supervision for filtering noisy retrieval. We propose silver-evidence demonstrations, which replace raw retrieved passages in ICL examples with generated, target-conditioned evidence summaries. For each labeled development example, an LLM generates silver evidence without access to the expert label or gold evidence; this evidence is then paired with the expert label and gold evidence where available. At test time, a single structured call generates silver evidence from retrieved passages and then predicts the final label and decision evidence. Across EI 2.0, SciFact, synthetic policy retrieval, and HICRIC/IMR data, our full method improves over equally sized gold-only ICL (label-only for policy) on three of four datasets and improves evidence F1 on all annotated datasets. It also achieves higher mean label accuracy than InstructRAG-style ICL on all four datasets. These results suggest that replacing demonstration-side retrieved passages with compact, target-conditioned silver evidence is particularly useful for decisions based on long and noisy text, where it reduces distracting context while preserving decision-relevant signals and expert supervision.

items.title: From Policy to Pedagogy: A Scoping Review of Artificial Intelligence Implementation Frameworks in Africa Universities
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly influencing higher education through its potential to support teaching, learning, assessment, research, and academic administration. Across Africa, AI offers opportunities to improve educational access, personalise learning, strengthen research capacity, and develop digital competencies. However, realising these benefits requires policies and implementation frameworks that address ethical use, academic integrity, data protection, infrastructure, digital inequalities, and staff and student competencies. The African Union’s Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy provides a continental direction for responsible, inclusive, and development-orientated AI adoption, while the African Union’s Digital Education Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023–2028 support the broader integration of digital technologies into education (African Union, 2024a, 2022).

items.title: From print to algorithm: teaching Indonesian postcolonial fiction with critical algorithmic literacy
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how Indonesian postcolonial fiction – principally Pramoedya Ananta Toer's Bumi Manusia [This Earth of Mankind] and Laksmi Pamuntjak's Amba – was taught across print, digitised and algorithmically mediated environments in two undergraduate English Language Teaching (ELT) literature courses in Surakarta and Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and what teaching critical algorithmic literacy looks like in such courses.Design/methodology/approach A qualitative multiple-case study drew on Indonesian postcolonial criticism, cultural memory studies and work on algorithmic and AI literacy, distinguishing three layers of mediation: digitised reading, algorithmic curation and generative AI. Data comprised classroom observation, instructor interviews, student focus groups and interviews, reflective journals and student-produced ‘feed audits’, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis by an author team that includes the courses’ own teacher.Findings Print-first close reading supported textual warranting and cultural-memory work; students perceived recommendation panels as foregrounding Anglophone titles over Indonesian ones; instructor-designed counter-searches and feed audits made algorithmic curation an object of critique; digital tools supported translanguaging across Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and English when paired with evaluation criteria; and hybrid sequencing was valued but labour-intensive.Originality/value The study's innovation is pedagogical rather than technological: a resource-aware, print-first sequence of feed audits, Indonesian-language counter-searches, checklists for generative AI output and evidence ladders that turns algorithms into objects of literary inquiry. It brings Indonesian literary criticism and language politics into dialogue with algorithmic literacy and identifies the conditions under which such teaching may be sustainable in Indonesian higher education.

items.title: From Promises to Accountability: Comparative AI Modeling and Visualization of Electoral Commitments in Nepali Political Texts
items.abstract: Election Commitment Mining refers to the analysis of election commitments made by electoral candidates or political parties during election campaigns. However, many elected candidates and political parties, especially in developing South Asian countries, do not fully deliver on the promises they make before elections. Even after the elections, commitments presented through election manifestos, posters, pamphlets, videos, and other campaign materials are often not systematically or transparently archived. As a result, these promises tend to fade away over time, making it difficult to hold the elected candidates accountable for their commitments. To address this persistent issue, this research aims to develop a system capable of structuring the commitments made by candidates during election periods. In this work, we created the first gold-standard dataset of Nepali political texts (Cohen's kappa = 0.777) and evaluated machine learning, deep learning and large language models to automatically extract and analyze election commitments. LaBSE-LR achieved the best results among machine learning models (0.897 accuracy, 0.896 macro F1-score, 0.947 AUROC), while fastText-LSTM achieved the highest performance among deep learning models (0.914 accuracy, 0.913 macro F1-score, 0.961 AUROC). Among the three evaluated large language models, Qwen3-8B performed best in the few-shot setting (0.848 macro F1-score). The outcome of this work is integrated into a mobile application, where commitments can be visualized with the support of GAI, enhancing transparency, civic engagement, and electoral accountability.

items.title: From Responsible Leadership to Responsible AI Governance: A Leadership-Based Framework for AI Governance in Organizations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizational decision-making, managerial roles, and accountability, yet responsible AI governance remains dominated by principles, technical controls, and regulatory compliance. This conceptual paper develops a human leadership-based framework for translating responsible AI principles into organizational governance. In the framework, the responsible leader is an accountable human organizational actor—such as a board member, senior executive, business leader, or designated decision owner—while AI is treated as a governed technological system or operational agent rather than the accountable leader. Human responsible leadership influences responsible AI governance (RAIG) capability through six mediating organizational processes: stakeholder orientation, ethical sensemaking, accountability architecture, meaningful human oversight, inclusive participation, and long-term value orientation. RAIG capability is defined as the higher-order organizational capacity to institutionalize and adapt lifecycle governance arrangements; it enables observable governance practices, which are conceptually separated from downstream responsible AI outcomes. AI operational autonomy is proposed as a focal moderator: the leadership-to-RAIG pathway should become stronger when AI can initiate or execute consequential actions with limited contemporaneous human approval, particularly where actions are difficult to reverse, trace, or interrupt. The framework offers testable propositions and a research agenda, but it is conceptual and requires empirical validation; it is not a technical safety guarantee.

items.title: From simulation to pedagogy: multi-model and randomized evaluation of structured AI standardized patients
items.abstract: Standardized patients (SPs) are central to clinical communication training but remain constrained by cost, scalability, and reliance on trained actors. We present AI standardized patients (AI-SPs), large language model–driven patient simulators built on a three-layer information architecture that adaptively modulates information disclosure according to learner skill. In Phase 1, blinded expert assessment of 350 simulated consultations generated by five frontier LLMs showed that, under a common architecture, learner skill level accounted for more of the observed performance variation than model choice ( η 2 = 0.31 vs. 0.06); whether this reflects the architecture itself cannot be determined without comparing models with and without it. In Phase 1b, analysis of 155 live student consultations identified systematic failures to elicit safety-critical information, enabling automated curriculum diagnostics without expert observation. In a Phase 2 three-arm pilot randomized study ( n = 58), OSCE performance gains with AI-SP training did not differ significantly from those with human SP training; the trial was designed to estimate effect sizes for a future confirmatory study, not to demonstrate equivalence. Self-efficacy gains were numerically largest with AI-SP training, but this exploratory difference did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. These findings suggest that architecture-driven AI-SPs could provide a scalable, model-portable approach to clinical communication training.

items.title: From Technology Readiness to Technical Competence
items.abstract: Purpose: The digital transformation in accounting, driven by automation and artificial intelligence, has reinforced the importance of technical skills, particularly in terms of technological adaptation in the training of future professionals. In this context, this study analyses the relation between the technological readiness of higher education students and their perception of technical readiness across the 12 competency areas operationalised from the International Education Standard 2 (IES 2) of the International Federation of Accountants (IFAC). Method: The research adopts a quantitative approach, based on a structured questionnaire administered to 146 students. The survey comprised three core components: sociodemographic data, self-assessment of technical readiness across the 12 IES 2 competency areas, and application of the Technology Readiness Index (TRI 2.0). Data analysis involved descriptive statistics, reliability analysis and Spearman’s correlations, with the aim of examining the association between technological readiness and the perception of technical competencies. Main Results: Based on the TRI 2.0 model by Parasuraman and Colby (2015), the results reveal a profile characterised by high optimism, moderate innovativeness, relatively low discomfort and high insecurity, reflecting a moderate overall level of technological readiness. At the same time, students report an overall positive perception of their technical readiness, with higher scores in financial accounting and reporting, information and communication technologies, and taxation, and lower scores in auditing. However, no statistically significant association was observed between overall technological readiness and the overall perception of technical competence. Nevertheless, a positive and significant relation was identified between overall technological readiness and competence in information and communication technologies. Key Conclusions: It is concluded that technological readiness does not automatically translate into a high overall perception of technical competence, although it appears to be associated with areas more directly related to the use of technology. The results reinforce the importance of pedagogical strategies that link the development of technical skills with technological adaptation, in a professional context increasingly marked by technological demands.

items.title: From the Soul Life of the Creator to the Black Box of the AI Chatbot: How to Close the Attribution Gap of AI Output?
items.abstract: Abstract This article addresses the profound legal dilemma posed by Generative AI within the contemporary art scene, arguing that German copyright law must focus not only on the work’s inherent object qualities but in particular on the human’s demonstrable concrete control over the output. When artists input hyper-complex prompt chains into AI tools like Midjourney or DALL-E to generate a picture, the essential question arises: Who owns the result? This legal challenge is twofold: an attribution crisis and a transparency crisis. Because the AI autonomously produces works without the required link to a human author’s personality, it creates a fundamental attribution gap. The challenge is no longer merely about the work itself, but about establishing a verifiable human influence amid the AI’s ‘black box’ processes. This analysis explores this critical question by examining the chain of attribution across three distinct stages of human influence over the AI process: Architecture/Training Data (Upstream), Prompting (Direct), and Post-processing (Downstream).

items.title: Future Perspectives on Digital Forensics and Cyber Security
items.abstract: As we entered the twenty-first century, we have witnessed an astonishing explosion of digital data, accompanied by a notable increase in the complexity and frequency of cyberattacks. The current cybersecurity landscape is grappling with challenges stemming from an ever-growing attack surface, driven by the widespread adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, the shift to cloud-based systems, and the increasing sophistication of cybercriminals. Meanwhile, digital forensics experts are inundated with petabytes of data, often struggling to navigate through vast, fragmented digital repositories to find critical evidence within tight legal timeframes. This disconnect between the overwhelming volume of digital interactions and the capacity for thorough human investigations highlights the need for a significant change in our approach. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is swiftly reshaping the fields of digital forensics and cybersecurity. This paper explores the latest AI applications, sheds light on emerging trends, and forecasts major advancements by 2035. Key areas of focus include automated evidence sorting, adversarial AI threats, quantum-resistant forensics, and ethical governance frameworks. By tapping into insights from machine learning, generative models, and explainable AI, we outline a roadmap for building robust and trustworthy systems. We also tackle challenges such as data bias, legal admissibility, and talent shortages, along with strategies to overcome them. Ultimately, this analysis underscores the importance of proactive, interdisciplinary collaboration to fully leverage AI’s potential while ensuring that justice and security remain intact.

items.title: Future-Ready Skills for Special Education Teachers in the Digital Era
items.abstract: The accelerating digitalization of schooling has reframed what it means to teach learners with disabilities. Special education teachers are now expected to combine traditional pedagogical expertise with assistive technology fluency, data literacy, and the socio-emotional sensitivity demanded by inclusive classrooms. This article presents a systematic literature review (SLR) that maps the future-ready skills required by special education teachers in the digital era. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 protocol, the search was conducted across three databases, namely Scopus, ScienceDirect, and EBSCO, using a Boolean string built around the constructs of future skills, special education teachers, and the digital era. After identification (n = 563), screening, and eligibility assessment, sixteen empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025 in indexed journals were retained for thematic synthesis. The analysis surfaced five interrelated competency clusters: (1) digital and assistive technology skills, (2) inclusive pedagogical skills, (3) socio-emotional and behavioral skills, (4) lifelong learning and adaptability, and (5) collaboration and interdisciplinary skills. Bibliometric mapping revealed concentration in Spain, the United States, and Indonesia, with the DigCompEdu and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) frameworks dominating conceptualization. Persistent gaps include the under-representation of low-resource contexts, fragmented teacher-preparation pathways, and limited integration of artificial intelligence within special education programs. The review contributes a competency synthesis that can inform curricular reform, professional development design, and policy aimed at preparing teachers who can deliver equitable, technology-enhanced instruction to learners with diverse needs.

items.title: Gallstone Disease Prediction With Explainable Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Gallstone disease (GSD) is one of the most frequently encountered digestive disorders in adults, and it often stays silent until it produces pain, infection or blockage of the bile ducts. Because its early symptoms overlap with many other abdominal conditions, a timely and confident diagnosis is not always possible, and imaging is not available at every point of care. This work presents a machine learning frameworsk that estimates gallstone risk from routinely recorded demographic, bioelectrical impedance and blood test parameters, and that explains every prediction it makes. A public dataset of 319 patients from the UCI repository is cleaned, scaled and encoded, after which four feature configurations are prepared: all attributes, attributes chosen through a correlation heatmap, attributes ranked by the ANOVA F-test, and the overlap of the last two. Seven classifiers, namely Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression, AdaBoost, Decision Tree and a Bagging ensemble, are trained under stratified five-fold cross-validation, giving 28 model–configuration pairs in total. The Support Vector Machine trained on correlation-selected features gives the strongest result, with 83.33% accuracy, 85.42% sensitivity and an area under the ROC curve of 88.80%. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) are then attached to this model. Both methods point to Vitamin D, C-reactive protein, bone mass, aspartate aminotransferase and hepatic fat grade as the dominant drivers of risk. The outcome is a transparent, low-cost screening aid that can help physicians flag likely gallstone cases early and understand why the system reached each decision.

items.abstract: The article examines gamification as a means of developing the pedagogical competence of future teachers. Gamification is treated not merely as a motivational device but as a two-level learning experience: students first participate in a gamified course and then design game elements for school learners. A "double-loop gamification" model, a table mapping game elements onto components of pedagogical competence, and methodological recommendations for pedagogical higher education institutions in Uzbekistan are proposed. The risk of undermining intrinsic motivation is discussed separately.

items.title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
items.abstract: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $α/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $α_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.

items.title: Generative AI and health misinformation: a lifecycle-based communication framework
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in the contemporary health information environment, where it can both generate and mitigate misinformation. Objective This review develops a Lifecycle-Based Framework to provide an integrative account of how generative AI operates across the health misinformation lifecycle from misinformation production and detection to correction and impact. Methods A narrative integrative review was conducted, drawing on research from communication science, public health, human-computer interaction, and artificial intelligence. Results The review identifies domain-specific mechanisms through which generative AI operates across the health misinformation lifecycle. In production, AI enables scalable generation of fluent, expert-styled content through mechanisms including hallucination, amplification of falsehoods, adversarial vulnerability, and deepfakes. In detection, it supports automated fact-checking, pattern recognition, and classification, while remaining vulnerable to false positives, false negatives, bias, and adversarial adaptation. In correction, generative AI facilitates rebuttals, tailored messaging, conversational engagement, and AI-assisted inoculation, but also raises concerns about trust displacement, epistemic authority, and accountability. At the impact stage, AI-mediated misinformation can influence individual cognition and behavior as well as broader social and institutional outcomes, with fluency, narrative coherence, and personalization serving as important persuasive mechanisms. The framework further conceptualizes the lifecycle as recursive and adaptive, such that production, detection, correction, and impact continually shape one another. Conclusion Generative AI should be understood not as a single source of misinformation risk, but as a multifunctional component of a dynamic health communication system. Addressing AI-mediated health misinformation therefore requires coordinated, multilevel strategies that account for its simultaneous roles in producing, detecting, correcting, and shaping the consequences of misinformation, while preserving human oversight, institutional accountability, and public trust.

items.title: Generative AI and Meaning-Making in Media and Communication: A Systematic Review of Semiotic Perspectives (2021–2026)
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping media and communication, yet research on its semiotic role in meaning-making remains theoretically and methodologically fragmented. This systematic review examines semiotic frameworks, technological modalities, communication contexts, and human–AI agency in research published from 2021 to 26 August 2026. Scopus and Web of Science searches identified 376 records; the final included corpus comprises 128 studies. The synthesis distinguishes between modality-specific concerns: studies of large language models primarily examine interaction and dialogue, whereas text-to-image studies emphasize representation and synthetic imagery. The RAW agency data contained four cases coded as predominantly AI-led, but these classifications changed following a documented text-consistency review, showing that the agency pattern is sensitive to coding decisions. We derive four provisional configurations: instrumental human anchoring, mediated distributed semiosis, co-creative/agentive participation, and contested or unresolved computational semiosis. The studies also reveal interconnected methodological, conceptual, cultural, technological, and governance gaps. These findings suggest that participation in sign production and mediation should be distinguished from claims of autonomous intentional agency; they do not establish whether generative systems possess intentional understanding.

items.title: Generative AI for STATA
items.abstract: This chapter explores the practical integration of Generative AI (Gen AI) into applied econometrics workflows using STATA. It introduces leading large language models (LLMs)—ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and LLaMA—and compares their capabilities for econometric applications. Core use cases are demonstrated: using Gen AI for teaching and learning complex concepts, guiding model selection and diagnostics, and generating advanced STATA syntax such as rolling-window Boone Index construction. A structured guide to prompt engineering emphasizes clarity, context, and task specificity. The chapter concludes with critical cautionary notes on code verification, AI hallucinations, and ethical citation practices, positioning Gen AI as a collaborative—not substitutive—research tool.

items.title: Generative AI in Second Language Video Composing: Investigating Students' Critical Digital Literacies and Multimodal Redesign
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in digital multimodal composing (DMC) presents both opportunities and challenges for second language (L2) research and pedagogy. While GenAI tools provide linguistic and multimodal support, they also raise concerns about biased information, culturally generic outputs, and technological overreliance. This qualitative study investigates L2 students' enactment of critical digital literacies (CDL) during GenAI‐assisted video composing. Drawing on CDL as a theoretical orientation and the analytical heuristic of critical awareness, critical identities, critical relationships, and critical actions, the study examines how students negotiated and revised AI‐generated video representations. Using multimodal critical discourse analysis of screen recordings, final video artifacts, focus group interviews, and reflective essays from 20 L2 students, the findings reveal four interrelated forms of CDL enactment. Students demonstrated critical awareness of GenAI's culturally limited outputs, authored critical identities through multimodal redesign, negotiated critical relationships with peers and GenAI, and engaged in localized critical action against cultural erasure. However, students' varied responses also highlight the uneven opportunities for CDL enactment across student groups. These findings offer theoretical and pedagogical implications for supporting L2 learners' critical engagement with algorithmic assumptions, cultural biases, and multimodal representations in GenAI‐assisted DMC.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Formation of Future Communication Professionals- Student Perceptions, Semiotic Mediation and Educational Challenges
items.abstract: The growing presence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in universities is transforming how academic knowledge is accessed, interpreted, and processed by students. Students increasingly rely on AI-based systems to retrieve information, summarize large volumes of content, clarify complex concepts and support academic writing. While these tools can improve speed, accessibility and day-to-day study support, they also raise difficult questions about intellectual autonomy, authorship, evaluation and the cultivation of critical reasoning. This paper explores the educational and professional implications of GenAI for future communication specialists. The study combines a qualitative exploratory investigation of student perceptions with a narrative literature review of recent academic work on AI in higher education. The empirical component was conducted with 20 undergraduate students enrolled in communication-related and engineering programs at the University of Medicine, Pharmacy, Sciences and Technology “George Emil Palade” in Târgu Mureș. Data were collected through semi-structured questions and analyzed through an inductive thematic coding procedure. The findings indicate that students perceive GenAI primarily as a practical learning assistant capable of translating dense academic content into more accessible explanations. At the same time, they express concerns regarding dependency, superficial learning, weakened independent effort and the authenticity of assessment. The paper argues that GenAI should not be treated as a substitute for human cognition, but as a mediated and reflexive instrument that can support intellectual formation when used transparently, critically and ethically. For communication education, this means preparing students not only to operate AI tools effectively, but also to question their outputs, interpret their symbolic effects and integrate them responsibly within professional communication practice.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence in medical oncology: A clinically focused narrative review of large language, vision‐language, and agentic artificial intelligence systems
items.abstract: Abstract Rapid advances in cancer genetics and genomics, pathophysiology, diagnostics, and therapeutics have substantially increased the complexity of clinical oncology. Integrating large and diverse data streams into timely, patient‐specific decisions provides a compelling rationale for incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into cancer care. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) encompasses several classes of models capable of generating new content. This clinically focused review concentrates on GenAI applications based primarily on large language models (LLMs) and vision‐language models (VLMs), as well as emerging agentic systems that use these models to perform coordinated, multistep tasks. LLMs demonstrate substantial medical knowledge, strong performance on oncology‐related assessments, and emerging capabilities in clinical reasoning. Guideline‐ and retrieval‐augmented systems can improve concordance with expert recommendations and interpretation of complex treatment algorithms. LLMs and VLMs have been applied to documentation, patient communication, information extraction and summarization, clinical decision support, and multimodal data synthesis. However, performance varies substantially across tasks and clinical domains, with important limitations including incomplete or outdated information, training‐data bias, automation bias, and confabulation. Agentic AI represents an emerging extension of these technologies in which LLMs or VLMs are incorporated into systems capable of multistep planning, external information retrieval, specialized tool use, and iterative evaluation and refinement. Early oncology applications include evidence synthesis, multimodal clinical decision support, radiology, pathology, surgery, and individualized treatment planning. With rigorous validation, transparent implementation, continual updating, and appropriate expert oversight, GenAI may augment oncologists’ judgment, improve patient understanding and experience, streamline cancer care delivery, and advance personalized oncology.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence in the preparation of scientific medical articles on surgery: principles of responsible use and current requirements of editorial organisations
items.abstract: Background. The rapid adoption of large language models between 2022 and 2026 has transformed the routine preparation of scientific manuscripts. In surgery, where the author is simultaneously a practising clinician with limited time for analytical work and is often compelled to publish results in English, the temptation to delegate text preparation to generative tools is particularly high. At the same time, leading editorial organisations have restricted the permissible scenarios for the use of artificial intelligence and tightened the requirements for disclosing such use.Objective. To systematise the current positions of editorial organisations regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence in scientific manuscripts, to outline the functional classes of tools relevant to surgical writing, and to formulate a practical framework for the responsible use of artificial intelligence, suitable for implementation in a surgeon’s daily scientific work.Materials and methods. A narrative literature review involving a targeted search of the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar databases for the period from January 2022 to July 2026, with restrictions on language (English, Ukrainian) and source type (peer-reviewed articles, official position papers from editorial organisations, and guidance documents on disclosure). The formal PRISMA–ScR protocol was not applied.Results. The ICMJE, COPE and WAME have agreed on three key positions regarding artificial intelligence: artificial intelligence cannot be an author; human authors bear full responsibility for the accuracy, integrity and originality of scientific manuscripts; and the use of artificial intelligence must be disclosed. The main clinically significant risks are the fabrication of references, factual inaccuracies in a medical context, bias, model drift, lack of reproducibility and breaches of patient data confidentiality. Automated detectors and expert assessment of content generated using artificial intelligence have limited reliability, which highlights the importance of voluntary disclosure of the use of artificial intelligence.Conclusions. Generative artificial intelligence should be regarded as an editorial and structural tool rather than a source of evidence. Responsible use of artificial intelligence requires mandatory verification of every statement and reference, de-identification of data, compliance with applicable guidelines on reporting, and transparent disclosure in the ‘Methods’ and ‘Acknowledgements’ sections.

items.title: Governing artificial intelligence for educational justice: developing a framework for inclusive and ethical digital learning
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) can be governed to advance educational justice, inclusion and ethical digital learning. It addresses incomplete integration across AI-in-education, AI-governance and educational-justice scholarship by developing a justice-oriented governance framework. Design/methodology/approach The study uses conceptual theory-building through an integrative synthesis of 186 sources identified through database searching and citation tracking for 2015–2025, with 2026 literature used only as contextual updates. The synthesis compares concepts, governance functions and theoretical relationships across domains. Findings The synthesis conceptualizes the AI–Justice Paradox as the possibility that expanded AI-enabled educational opportunity may coexist with or intensify injustice. It develops the educational justice governance framework (EJGF), comprising equitable access, capability development, algorithmic fairness, participatory governance and accountability and rights protection. These dimensions are theorized as conditionally interdependent and partially non-substitutable. Originality/value The contribution is integrative and relational: the EJGF complements established cross-sector AI-governance approaches by specifying educational justice as the substantive criterion linking governance safeguards within educational institutions. The framework is conceptually derived and requires empirical validation across contexts, institutions and AI applications. It also generates testable propositions concerning configurational relationships and boundary conditions.

items.title: GPT Deprivation: How the Wrong Point on the Ontology and Expectations Scale Leads to Losses from Generative AI. A Multiple-Case Study, 2023–2026
items.abstract: Why do people and organizations lose money, health, reputation and jobs when they rely on generative AI? This study tests the claim that publicly documented losses from LLM chat applications (2023–2026) are explained less by model defects than by a gap between the assigned and the actual nature of the system. The gap runs along two axes: ontology, meaning what kind of system the user takes it for, and expectations, meaning what the user believes it can do in a given task. Data and method. The study is a multiple-case study in the logic of accident investigation. It draws on four datasets: 9 incidents with a loss to a specific person or organization, plus 3 population-level markers; a comparative corpus of 17 units; a random sample of 30 court cases from the AI Hallucination Cases database; a census of 33 lawsuits by users and their families against chat-application vendors. Vendor announcements of 14 model launches are analyzed alongside these datasets. The sources are court documents, peer-reviewed publications, reports and media. Units are coded in three layers: two independent coders, author review and, on key features, an independent human coder. The standard of proof is existence and severity: one documented irreversible case establishes the pattern for a party, and statistical power is not a criterion. Findings. Courts sanction the failure to verify AI output, not the use of AI itself. In lawsuits against general-purpose assistants, trust transfer is the main described path to harm: trust earned on everyday, study and work tasks carries over to a domain where the user lacks competence. This holds in 21 of the 22 lawsuits where the path can be established. A failed barrier is found in all 7 main-corpus incidents where the loss passed through trust in the model's answer, in 9 of 10 comparative-corpus incidents and in 17 of 28 sampled court cases. For users, vendors and professional filers, at least one case with a violated element reached irreversible and significant harm. No case was found in which the duty to verify was fulfilled and the error still reached the decision. The loss does not occur at the moment of the model's error. It occurs at one of two points. The first is when an unverified answer becomes an irreversible action. The second is when the user or operator discovers that money, compute, time or jobs were spent and the goal was not achieved. In both cases the breach lies in the discipline of use, which the study calls "use diplomacy": assigning the tool's purpose and the bounds of trust before the work begins. Contents of this record. The main report, written in English as the original, with a Ukrainian version. A companion study of hypothesis H4: "Companion or Tool: The Relational Tuning of LLM Chat Applications". The codebook, the coder instructions, the preregistration and the deviations log. Case dossiers with verbatim quotations from primary sources. Coded datasets, the original codes of every coder, agreement reports and selection logs. A recomputation script and an external verification package. English files carry no language suffix. Ukrainian files carry the suffix .ua and sit in the ua/ folder, for example ua/codebook.ua.md. The Ukrainian dossiers and the Ukrainian deviations log are machine translations; this is marked in their titles. The coding algorithm is published, so the coding can be reproduced with any coders. Limitations. A corpus of public incidents does not permit frequency estimates, and the results are exploratory. Cases where an error was caught before it reached a decision are not documented, so the effectiveness of each barrier cannot be measured with this method.

items.title: GPT-4 reasons like infants about objects but not agents
items.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is central to human social cognition and is critical for successfully navigating the social world. However, most work to date has explored explicit ToM in AI, particularly with large language models (LLMs), and has found mixed results. In contrast, decades of developmental psychology research with human infants has found remarkable, early-emerging implicit ToM. However, little work has explored implicit ToM in LLMs. The current study investigates implicit social reasoning abilities in GPT-4 using model-facing versions of classic infant experiments. In Experiment 1, we explored GPT-4’s implicit ToM abilities across four social reasoning tasks adapted from infant paradigms. In Experiment 2, we explored whether GPT-4 was capable of physical reasoning to contrast with social reasoning in Experiments 1 and 2. Across these three experiments, our results suggest that there may be domain differences in GPT-4’s reasoning abilities, such that GPT-4 struggled with social reasoning tasks despite performing very well on physical reasoning tasks. These findings highlight the importance of systematic exploration of social reasoning in LLMs and provide insight into potential deficits in GPT-4’s social reasoning abilities.

items.title: Graduated Autonomy for Artificial Intelligence Agents in Human Capital Management: A Systematic Review and a Consequence-Calibrated Governance Framework
items.abstract: Human capital management platforms are starting to embed software agents built on large language models. Unlike earlier analytics tools, these agents can plan a sequence of steps, call system functions and change employee records. Artificial intelligence is therefore moving from advising managers to acting for them. Most governance guidance, however, was written for systems that recommend rather than act. This study asks how organisations should match the autonomy of such agents to the consequences of the people decisions they touch. A systematic review was conducted and reported using the PRISMA 2020 guideline. Eighteen structured searches of a multi-source scholarly index returned 180 records. After duplicate removal and eligibility screening, 55 peer-reviewed sources were retained, and four foundational and regulatory sources were added. Thematic synthesis produced seven findings. Algorithmic control of work is already extensive. Bias in hiring tools is persistent and partly organisational. Human review is weaker than assumed, because reviewers often defer to machine advice. Responsibility tends to diffuse as systems gain autonomy. Employee trust depends on fair process and visible human involvement. Language-model agents add new failure modes, such as fabricated content and hidden instructions planted in documents. Finally, current governance frameworks rarely specify controls for individual delegated actions. Building on these findings, the study proposes a consequence-calibrated governance framework. It sets an autonomy ceiling for each class of people decision and links every ceiling to five control layers. Six testable propositions and practical guidance for human resource and technology leaders are offered. Keywords: large language models; people analytics; algorithmic management; automation bias; meaningful human control

items.title: Green Code or Costly Code? Evaluating the Energy Costs of Iterative LLM-Based Code Optimizations
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to optimize code for performance. This practice often assumes that improvements in execution speed naturally translate into overall lower energy consumption. We challenge this assumption empirically by measuring whether performance-optimized code produced by LLM self-refinement pipelines is also energy-efficient relative to canonical human reference solutions, and whether the energy cost of the optimization process can be offset by subsequent execution-time savings. We evaluate 11 open-source models across four decoding configurations on all 1,000 problems of EffiBench, a state-of-the-art performance benchmark, while collecting per-process, hardware-level energy measurements throughout. Inference energy spans 0.79 to 8.68 MJ across model-variant pairs, which is roughly equivalent to the energy of 250 to 2800 GPT-4.1 queries. Limiting the maximum number of output tokens has the largest impact, reducing energy use by up to 69% compared to the default configuration. On the execution side, 42 of 44 configurations produce code that consumes more energy per problem than the canonical human reference, with overheads ranging from +4% to +886%. The two exceptions achieve only marginal gains, with break-even points on the order of 10^6 to 10^7 executions. Mixture-of-Experts architectures consume substantially less inference energy than equivalently-sized dense models without sacrificing correctness, making architectural choice a more consequential sustainability lever than decoding parameters. Performance optimization and energy efficiency are not always aligned goals: LLM self-refinement consistently produces faster-seeking but energy-heavier code relative to what a human engineer would write. All artifacts are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598170.

items.title: Guided Zero-Shot Anomaly Explanation for Anonymized Crowd Video Monitoring: Context, Categorization, and Spatial Localization
items.abstract: Despite the promising development of deep learning for video anomaly detection (VAD), explainability (XAI) of these models remains a challenge. Explainable and privacy-protecting VAD builds transparency and trust that facilitates adoption of computer vision systems, including safety and security monitoring. However, anomaly explainability in privacy-preserving VAD systems is underexplored. In this study, we present the XAVAD approach, a unified descriptive anomaly XAI for an anonymized VAD, that integrates flexible zero-shot anonymization, anomaly type categorization, visual localization, and scene context description. We provide empirical and qualitative assessments of multifaceted explanations integrated with full-body visual anonymization for privacy protection. We adopt a multimodal CLIP embedding for videos, using improved LLM-assisted prompting and pool-scoring mechanisms for anomaly-type identification. We enhance Grad-ECLIP for spatial anomaly heatmap localization, leveraging computation and accuracy through our novel prompt-guided patching autofocus mechanism. We employ VLMs to generate context and reasoning descriptions of detected anomalies through curated prompt engineering. We have evaluated the accuracy and computational cost of XAVAD on several publicly available CCTV and video datasets. Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains of our XAVAD over state-of-the-art benchmark approaches and provide insights into privacy protection trade-offs in XAI for VAD. We further present ablation studies and assessments across diverse configurations and modeling alternatives to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods. items.title: He(Art) Meets AI
items.abstract: What if art were data? In clinical settings, pain and emotional distress are typically measured using numeric scales, yet patients often describe their suffering through metaphor, narrative, and image. This chapter examines the tension between standardized assessment and creative expression and explores how artificial intelligence (AI) might support a new dimension of care by rendering expressive forms legible as candidate clinical signals, pending validation in longitudinal, clinician-governed studies. Grounded in the interdisciplinary development of ICANFEEL, a digital art-based tool for symptom expression, we illustrate how creative outputs—including visual compositions, narrative language, and voice—can function as a complementary, multimodal layer of health information within patient-centered precision medicine. Drawing on case examples from psycho-oncology, we address the ethical and cultural implications of translating metaphor into medical contexts and consider future applications of AI in expressive therapies. Through practical illustrations and a guided creative exercise, this chapter invites readers to reconsider what counts as data in mental health, and how expressive arts, when thoughtfully paired with AI, may deepen care, insight, and clinical attunement.

items.title: Heart Rate Variability Analysis and Early Detection of Cardiac Conditions
items.abstract: Heart rate variability has emerged as a robust, non-invasive biomarker for assessing autonomic nervous system function and enabling early detection of cardiovascular disorders. This chapter presents a comprehensive analysis of HRV methodologies, including time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear measures, along with advances in biosignal acquisition using electrocardiography (ECG), photoplethysmography (PPG), and wearable sensors. The integration of lightweight artificial intelligence, machine learning, and IoT-enabled healthcare systems for real-time monitoring and predictive analytics is critically examined. Applications in detecting arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and stress-related conditions are discussed. Furthermore, challenges, ethical considerations, and emerging trends such as federated learning and digital twins are highlighted, emphasizing the potential of HRV-driven systems in advancing personalized and preventive cardiovascular healthcare.

items.title: Hierarchical Traffic State Fusion for Infrastructure Assisted Vehicle Speed Regulation of Autonomous Electric Vehicles
items.abstract: Abstract Infrastructure-assisted autonomous driving has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the situational awareness and operational efficiency of Autonomous Electric Vehicles (AEVs) in structured environments. However, existing studies often address traffic perception, wireless communication, and vehicle control as separate components, with limited emphasis on an integrated perception–communication–control framework for traffic-aware speed regulation. This paper presents a Hierarchical Traffic State Fusion Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (HTSF-V2I) framework that integrates multi-camera roadside traffic perception, edge artificial intelligence, long-range LoRa communication, onboard LiDAR sensing, and traffic-state-dependent vehicle speed regulation using a lightweight embedded architecture. Three roadside cameras equipped with an optimized lightweight YOLOv8-based detector monitor campus traffic and estimate local traffic states. A deterministic HTSF module combines the multi-camera traffic states into a unified infrastructure-level traffic advisory, which is transmitted to the AEV through LoRa-based V2I communication. Onboard LiDAR provides local obstacle verification and overrides the infrastructure-derived propulsion command when an obstacle is detected within the defined safety threshold. For smart-campus evaluation, a dataset comprising 5,914 manually annotated traffic images was developed for training and evaluating the traffic perception module. The standard YOLOv8n baseline achieved an mAP@50 of 88.3% at an input resolution of $$640\times 640$$ , whereas the deployed $$320\times 320$$ CampusLite configuration achieved an mAP@50 of 70.3%, providing a practical trade-off between detection accuracy and computational efficiency for embedded deployment. Experimental evaluation demonstrates multi-camera traffic perception, infrastructure-level traffic-state estimation, end-to-end LoRa-based traffic-advisory transmission, and vehicle propulsion-command selection using infrastructure-derived traffic information with local obstacle supervision. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating infrastructure perception, deterministic traffic-state fusion, wireless communication, and onboard safety intelligence within a lightweight framework for low-speed AEV operation in smart-campus environments. The proposed HTSF-V2I framework provides a computationally practical approach for infrastructure-assisted, traffic-aware speed regulation on resource-constrained embedded platforms.

items.title: High-throughput mass spectrometry-based metabolomics for large-scale population studies: technical barriers and recent innovations
items.abstract: Large-scale metabolomic studies are needed to identify and validate biomarkers for their successful translation in emerging population health and precision medicine initiatives. Yet, untargeted mass spectrometry (MS)-based metabolomics remains hampered by low sample throughput, limited coverage, complicated data processing, poor standardization, and high operating costs. These challenges also contribute to a reproducibility crisis, with most reported biomarkers not independently replicated, given variations in study designs, sample workup protocols, instrumental methods, and data pre-processing workflows. This review will focus on new advances in high-throughput MS platforms and computational software with emerging artificial intelligence/machine learning tools that are scalable, faster, and less prone to error. Recent progress to improve data harmonization in population-level metabolomic, lipidomic, and exposomic studies (n > 1000) will also be discussed. This will include strategies to correct for long-term batch effects, improve metabolite identification, and derive biochemical insights into disease mechanisms when integrated with multi-omic studies.

items.title: Homiletical Theory in Retrospect and Prospect
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter provides an overview of homiletical theories from the mid-twentieth century to the present and suggests future directions, taking account of emphases characteristic of preaching in particular social locations, for example, Eurocentric and African American. The chapter begins with a discussion of the meaning of “homiletical theory” and then turns to homiletical theories characteristic of four eras. In the mid-twentieth century, Eurocentric homiletics responded to issues raised by modernity while African American approaches centered more on empowering congregations to survive racism. In the last quarter of the twentieth century, the New Homiletic emerged in Eurocentric preaching theory as liberation approaches found footing in other communities and among Eurocentric feminists. In the early twenty-first century, scholars and preachers began to take account of preaching in light of the qualities essential to specific social locations, along with empirical studies of preaching. Issues for the future include decentering the whiteness of homiletical theory, the development of approaches to preaching outside the typical service of worship, the degree to which artificial intelligence could play a part in preaching, possibilities of learning from other disciplines, and the importance of homiletical theory serving the causes of justice.

items.title: How AI-Enabled Service Encounters Shape Tourist Trust: The Role of Perceived Personalization and Interactional Justice
items.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies increasingly mediate service encounters in tourism, understanding how AI-enabled interactions shape tourist trust has become a pressing issue. Drawing on social exchange theory and justice theory, this study investigates the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI service quality influences tourist trust. Using the AI digital human Wang Bo at the Tengwang Pavilion scenic area as an empirical case, the research develops and tests a model in which perceived personalization and interactional justice act as parallel mediators, while privacy sensitivity and brand reputation serve as moderators. Results from structural equation modeling show that AI service quality significantly enhances both perceived personalization and interactional justice, which in turn foster tourist trust. Perceived personalization and interactional justice each play significant mediating roles, indicating that tourists’ trust in AI arises not merely from technical performance but from perceptions of individualized care and fair treatment. Among the moderating effects, privacy sensitivity attenuates the relationship between AI service quality and interactional justice but does not affect the link between AI service quality and perceived personalization. Brand reputation strengthens the impact of perceived personalization on trust but does not significantly moderate the relationship between interactional justice and trust. Overall, the findings reveal dual pathways—personalization-based and fairness-based—through which AI service quality builds trust, highlighting the interplay between technological excellence, human-like social attributes, and contextual factors in shaping tourists’ trust toward AI-enabled services. items.title: How and When Artificial Intelligence Awareness Fosters Proactive Career Behaviors: The Role of Workplace Impostor Thoughts and Future Work Self Salience
items.abstract: Drawing on self-discrepancy theory, this study examined how and when artificial intelligence (AI) awareness promotes proactive career behaviors. We collected three-wave, time-lagged data from 329 full-time employees in the United Kingdom. Results showed that AI awareness was positively related to proactive career behaviors. The indirect effect of AI awareness on proactive career behaviors through workplace impostor thoughts was significant when future work self salience was high but not when it was low. Future work self salience also strengthened both the relationship between AI awareness and workplace impostor thoughts and the direct relationship between AI awareness and proactive career behaviors. These findings demonstrate that technology-induced identity threats can motivate proactive career efforts and clarify how and when AI awareness translates into proactive career behaviors. Implications for career counseling and organizational practice are discussed.

items.title: How does community of inquiry matter? Mediating effects and configurational pathways linking project-based learning design to learning engagement
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) has reshaped animation students’ skill profiles and the conditions of instructional design in project-based learning (PBL) studios. We examine whether and how perceptions of PBL design are associated with Learning Engagement (LE), treating AIGC-assisted PBL studios as the research context rather than testing generative AI as a model variable. Drawing on Community of Inquiry (CoI) theory, we examine Problem Driven (PD), Project Design (PDe), Project Implementation (PI), and Project Evaluation (PE) as antecedents; Cognitive Presence (CP), Social Presence (SP), and Teaching Presence (TP) as statistical mediators; and LE as the outcome. We analyzed two-wave survey data from 490 upper-year animation students using PLS-SEM and fsQCA. PBL and CoI were measured concurrently at T1, and LE at T2; indirect effects therefore represent indirect statistical associations rather than mediation with a fully established temporal sequence. PD, PDe, and PI showed significant positive direct associations with LE. PE’s zero-order and single-predictor associations were positive, but its direct path coefficient became significantly negative after controlling for the other PBL dimensions and CoI mediators. The coefficient was sensitive to model specification, suggesting possible statistical suppression; it should not be interpreted as evidence that evaluation itself inherently inhibits engagement. The three CoI dimensions showed significant statistical mediation associations across all 12 indirect paths. TP and SP had relatively higher point estimates of indirect statistical associations, but differences between indirect effects were not formally tested; no dimension is claimed to be optimal. PE’s positive indirect associations through CoI partially offset its negative net direct association without reversing the total association after adjustment. The extent of this offset may depend on the degree to which CoI-related experiences are concurrently reported. fsQCA identified seven high-engagement configurations. No individual PBL dimension was indispensable. CoI dimensions appeared as core or peripheral conditions, although not every configuration included all three. These findings clarify the dual pathways linking evaluation and engagement through indirect statistical associations and configurational conditions, and provide guidance for optimizing PBL under different resource constraints. Conclusions are limited to AIGC-assisted PBL studios and do not establish the instructional effects of generative AI.

items.title: How Large Language Models Weight Narrative Cues When Detecting Deception in Oral Accounts: A Multi‐Model Comparison
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Lie detection research has increasingly turned to artificial intelligence, yet the application of large language models (LLMs) remains underexplored for transcribed oral narratives. We compared five LLMs (Gemini‐3‐flash, Gemini‐3‐pro, Deepseek‐v4‐flash, GPT‐5.6‐luna, and Grok‐4) in classifying truthful and deceptive statements from interview transcripts of oral travel narratives collected from 95 Chinese‐speaking participants. Guided by Criteria‐Based Content Analysis (CBCA), Reality Monitoring (RM), and the Verifiability Approach (VA), theory‐driven prompts instructed models to score five narrative cues before making binary veracity judgments. Gemini‐3‐flash achieved the highest accuracy (74.74%, AUC = 0.76) with 81.63% sensitivity and 67.39% specificity, and stable repeated‐run performance. For this optimal model, unusual/superfluous details served as the sole significant predictor of objective veracity even after controlling for text length. LLMs can detect deception above chance but show large performance heterogeneity. Independent human coding, cross‐cultural replications, and adversarial robustness testing are needed before real‐world deployment.

items.title: How Peer Working Hours Shape Individual Preferences: Experimental Evidence From Germany
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how colleagues' working hours influence individual working hours preferences. We conducted a representative survey experiment among German employees in 2024, in which participants received randomized information about colleagues' working hours. We combine the survey experiment with quantitative and LLM‐based text analysis of an open‐ended question. Colleagues' hours causally influence stated preferences, yet respondents' explanations focus on personal reasons. This shows that social factors influence working time preferences alongside the individual considerations that respondents most frequently identify. Our findings highlight the importance of collective action for working‐time policy and reveal methodological considerations for studying labor supply preferences.

items.title: How postgraduate learning engagement in generative AI-assisted contexts supports critical thinking: A grounded theory study
items.abstract: Despite growing interest in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, limited attention has been paid to how learning engagement is reconfigured in GenAI-assisted contexts and how it supports critical thinking. This study adopts a grounded theory approach to examine the dimensions of postgraduate learning engagement and its underlying mechanisms. Based on semi-structured interviews with 32 postgraduates, four dimensions are identified: cognitive, emotional, human-AI interaction, and agentic engagement. Extending existing frameworks, the findings show that engagement promotes critical thinking through both direct and indirect pathways. Learning self-efficacy and lower-order cognitive offloading act as key mediators, while GenAI trust serves as a contextual moderator. A process-oriented model is proposed to explain how GenAI reshapes engagement and fosters higher-order thinking.
